source.title: Vectorizing string entries for data processing on tables: when are larger language models better?
source.authors: Léo Grinsztajn; Edouard Oyallon; M. Kim; G. Varoquaux

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether model scale or embedding quality predicts downstream task performance, using table analytics and fuzzy-join measures rather than language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates downstream performance of text embeddings from pretrained models, including comparisons by model size and embedding benchmark score. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit power laws, test extrapolation, or optimize parameter-token allocation. Its reference to Kaplan et al. is cited context, not a result from this study.
record.test_reason: The study compares downstream tabular-analytics performance (ROC-AUC gain over MinHash) across pretrained embedding models of different sizes (Fig. 5, Table II). That is a new-setting result on whether downstream performance improves with scale (V6). It does not measure pretraining loss, fit power laws, or vary compute or allocation, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested. The comparisons use existing model families, not a controlled training sweep.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add two points: within a model family bigger is better, and across families very large models bring no significant benefit over e5-v2. The authors attribute Pythia's weaker result to fewer training tokens.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates off-the-shelf text embedding models in tabular analytics and fuzzy joins; it does not reproduce a language-model pretraining scaling-law procedure or fit pretraining-loss curves.
record.method_sensitivity: Results depend on string diversity: the reported benefit from better embeddings appears for diverse entries but not dirty categories. Fine-tuned smaller models are competitive with larger models.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher MTEB average score corresponds to larger analytics gain for diverse-entry columns but not dirty-category columns (Fig. 4). It also corresponds to larger fuzzy-join F1 gain (Fig. 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream gains of text embeddings in table tasks track general embedding-benchmark quality only when column string diversity is high.

record.problems: The scale results use comparisons among existing model families rather than a controlled training sweep; model size, training data, architecture, and fine-tuning status vary. Several relevant figure values are not stated numerically in the text, and the paper does not establish a quantitative prediction law.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results specifically relating downstream performance to model size or embedding quality were identified for extraction. Other comparisons in the paper concern embedding methods or pipeline choices rather than the scale relationship in V6.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured, no power-law fit.
No controlled shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law form tested in other modalities or regimes.
Predictability from pretraining loss untested. No quantitative or functional fit of downstream performance vs size.
No fitted exponents or fitting choices compared.

missing.what: Per-model ROC-AUC and F1 gains with parameter counts. Examples: Llama-2-7b 4.0%, e5-large-v2 335M 3.77%, pythia-6.9b 2.81%, bge-micro 17.4M 1.03%.
Fuzzy-join F1 gain vs MTEB score (relevant only as non-scale context).

record.verdict_notes: The record's tranche should be T3 (new downstream setting), not T2. Scale evidence is observational across heterogeneous released models, so size is confounded with training data, architecture and fine-tuning. Kaplan et al. is only cited.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger-run pretraining loss.
No fixed-compute allocation of parameters and tokens.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The study applies text embeddings to tabular tasks but does not test scaling laws across modalities or training regimes.
Tests downstream task performance across embedding models and some size comparisons, but does not test predictability from pretraining loss or establish a quantitative predictive law.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits are compared across fitting choices, and no pretraining-loss curves are analyzed.

rows.subject: Model families compared in Figure 5 (aggregate within-family size trend)
rows.size_stated: Multiple sizes; individual sizes are not stated in the figure text.
rows.stage_stated: Pretrained embedding models; some models are fine-tuned for sentence embeddings.
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream analytics performance across embedding-model sizes, using MinHashEncoder as the reference.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error bars are shown, halved for readability.
rows.note: The authors state that within a given model family, larger models show clear gains and no observed plateau as size increases; they also note diminishing returns across models overall.
rows.check: Holds within model families only (e5, Pythia, etc.): authors see no plateau with size. Across families, Fig. 5 shows diminishing returns: very large models bring 'no significant benefits compared to e5-v2'. The cross-family part belongs with r4's limits_scope. Figure-only values.

rows.subject: Language-model embeddings (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Multiple model sizes; not stated for this result.
rows.stage_stated: Pretrained; includes models of differing fine-tuning status.
rows.operation_detail: Compared the downstream analytics benefit of better embedding models across columns with different string diversity.

conditions.value: Dirty categories; fewer than 3000 unique character n-grams per 1000 rows

rows.measure: Gain from better language-model embeddings on analytics tasks
rows.value: The authors report no gain from using better models in the dirty-categories regime; figure values not stated.
rows.note: This is a condition where better model benchmark performance does not translate into downstream gains.
rows.check: 'Better models' here means higher MTEB score, not larger scale or lower pretraining loss. It does not measure what V6 names, so it fits no version.

rows.subject: Language-model embeddings (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Multiple model sizes; not stated for this result.
rows.stage_stated: Pretrained; includes models of differing fine-tuning status.
rows.operation_detail: Compared embedding-model benchmark quality with downstream analytics performance across columns with different string diversity.

conditions.value: Diverse entries; more than 3000 unique character n-grams per 1000 rows

rows.measure: Relationship between MTEB average score and analytics performance gain over MinHashEncoder
rows.value: The authors report that better MTEB performance translates to better analytics performance in this regime; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: The paper reports a qualitative association; it does not provide a fitted prediction equation.
rows.check: This is a correlation between MTEB benchmark score and analytics gain. MTEB score is neither scale nor pretraining loss, so the row fits no version.

rows.subject: Small fine-tuned models (including bge and e5) compared with largest evaluated models
rows.stage_stated: Small models are fine-tuned for sentence embeddings; the largest-model group includes models not fine-tuned for sentence similarity.
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream analytics performance of small fine-tuned embedding models with the largest evaluated models.

conditions.value: Default analytics pipeline; see Table II and Figure 5

rows.measure: Analytics performance, including ROC-AUC gain over MinHashEncoder
rows.value: Small fine-tuned models achieve close or better performance; individual values are not stated in the accompanying text.
rows.locator: Section IV-C(c), Table II and Figure 5
rows.note: The reported comparison qualifies a general size-benefit interpretation: fine-tuning can make much smaller models competitive with the largest models.
rows.check: Baseline and subject are roughly right. Table II gives values: e5-large-v2 (335M) 3.77% vs Llama-2-7b 4.0%, Mistral-7B 3.93%, llama-7b 3.75%, pythia-6.9b 2.81%. So size alone does not predict gain across families.

relationships.condition: Within a model family (e.g. e5, Pythia), tabular analytics at 1000 training samples
relationships.reason: Fig. 5: within a family, larger models give clear ROC-AUC gains with no plateau (r1).
relationships.display_finding: ROC-AUC increased with model size within each family, with no observed plateau.

relationships.condition: Across model families differing in fine-tuning and training data
relationships.reason: Gains show diminishing returns. 335M fine-tuned e5/bge match or beat 7B models, and pythia-6.9b trails at 2.81% vs 4.0% (r1, r4, Table II).
relationships.display_finding: Fine-tuned 335M e5/bge models matched or beat 7B models, while pythia-6.9b trailed at 2.81% versus 4.0%, showing diminishing returns across families.
